```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Exercises graded on a value instead of the exact code.
# Add an entry here to opt an exercise in, using list(var) to check a variable,
# list(expr) to check a Python expression, or list(last_value = TRUE) to check the
# student's last line. The result is compared against the same thing computed from
# the exercise's -solution chunk; add value = ... to compare against a fixed number
# instead. Add defines = "name" to require the student's code to define that name
# itself. Add structure = c(...) to also require the code to have a certain shape
# (see check_structure below for the rules). Any exercise not listed is graded by
# exact code match against its -solution chunk.
value_checks <- list(
  # Any valid SRS passes: 15 values drawn from sleep_hours without reusing any (checked
  # by comparing value counts), sleep_mean is the mean of the student's own sample, and
  # the code sets replace=False
  srs_ex = list(expr = paste(
    'int(len(sleep_sample) == 15',
    'and not (__import__("collections").Counter(list(sleep_sample)) - __import__("collections").Counter(list(sleep_hours)))',
    'and bool(np.isclose(sleep_mean, np.mean(sleep_sample))))'),
    value = 1, defines = c("sleep_sample", "sleep_mean"), structure = "no_replace"),
  # Any valid stratified sample passes: 20 different, unchanged rows of dorm, 10 from each
  # year, and the code uses .sample() so the rows are picked at random
  strat_ex = list(expr = paste(
    'int(len(strat_sample) == 20',
    'and strat_sample.index.is_unique',
    'and bool(strat_sample.index.isin(dorm.index).all())',
    'and bool((strat_sample["year"].value_counts().reindex(["Freshman", "Sophomore"]) == 10).all())',
    'and strat_sample[["year", "sleep_hours"]].equals(dorm.loc[strat_sample.index, ["year", "sleep_hours"]]))'),
    value = 1, defines = "strat_sample", structure = "df_sample"),
  # Any valid cluster sample passes: unchanged rows of dorm_floors making up exactly 2 whole floors
  # (every resident on each chosen floor), and the code picks the floors at random
  cluster_ex = list(expr = paste(
    'int(cluster_sample.index.is_unique',
    'and bool(cluster_sample.index.isin(dorm_floors.index).all())',
    'and cluster_sample["floor"].nunique() == 2',
    'and set(cluster_sample.index) == set(dorm_floors.index[dorm_floors["floor"].isin(cluster_sample["floor"])])',
    'and cluster_sample.equals(dorm_floors.loc[cluster_sample.index]))'),
    value = 1, defines = "cluster_sample", structure = "cluster_random"),
  # The heat map must use the "magma" color map and still show the floor-by-year table
  heatmap_ex = list(expr = paste(
    'int(heatmap.get_cmap().name == "magma"',
    'and bool(np.allclose(heatmap.get_array(), dorm_floors.pivot_table(index="floor", columns="year", values="sleep_hours", aggfunc="mean").to_numpy())))'),
    value = 1, defines = "heatmap"),
  # The histogram must have 20 bins and include all 100 values of study_hours
  hist_bins_ex = list(expr = paste(
    'int(len(ax.patches) == 20',
    'and sum(bar.get_height() for bar in ax.patches) == len(study_hours)',
    'and min(bar.get_x() for bar in ax.patches) == study_hours.min())'),
    value = 1, defines = "ax"),
  # freshmen and sophomores must be the right rows of dorm_exams (row numbers can differ),
  # and the 24 sophomore points must be drawn in orange (any of matplotlib's oranges)
  scatter_color_ex = list(expr = paste(
    'int(freshmen.reset_index(drop=True).equals(dorm_exams[dorm_exams["year"] == "Freshman"].reset_index(drop=True))',
    'and sophomores.reset_index(drop=True).equals(dorm_exams[dorm_exams["year"] == "Sophomore"].reset_index(drop=True))',
    'and any(np.asarray(c.get_offsets()).shape[0] == 24',
    'and __import__("matplotlib").colors.to_hex(c.get_facecolor()[0]) in ("#ffa500", "#ff7f0e", "#ff8c00")',
    'and sorted(map(tuple, np.asarray(c.get_offsets()).round(3).tolist())) == sorted(map(tuple, dorm_exams.loc[dorm_exams["year"] == "Sophomore", ["sleep_hours", "exam_score"]].to_numpy().round(3).tolist()))',
    'for c in ax.collections))'),
    value = 1, defines = c("ax", "freshmen", "sophomores"))
)

# Python helpers for custom_checker (done in Python so they work the same on every
# Python version).
# get_result runs code like learnr does (setup objects visible, new variables kept
# separate) and returns the value being checked.
# values_match compares a student's result to the expected one. Data frames and
# series match if they have the same row labels and counts, ignoring their names,
# row order, and the outer level of the column labels (so values = "SID" and
# values = ["SID"] both work).
checker_py <- '
# (imports go inside the functions because py_run_string keeps top-level names local)
def get_result(code, var=None, expr=None, last_value=False, defines=()):
    import ast
    import __main__
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    if last_value:
        if not tree.body:
            raise ValueError("no code")
        last = tree.body[-1]
        if isinstance(last, ast.Assign) and len(last.targets) == 1 and isinstance(last.targets[0], ast.Name):
            # Last line is `name = expr`, so read `name`
            var = last.targets[0].id
        elif isinstance(last, ast.Expr):
            # Rewrite the last line `expr` as `__check_result__ = expr` so we can read it
            target = ast.Name(id="__check_result__", ctx=ast.Store())
            tree.body[-1] = ast.copy_location(ast.Assign(targets=[target], value=last.value), last)
            ast.fix_missing_locations(tree)
            var = "__check_result__"
        else:
            raise ValueError("last line is not an expression")
    user_vars = {}
    # Plotting code ends in plt.show(), which could try to open a window when run here, so
    # turn it off while the code runs and close the figures it made afterwards
    import sys
    pyplot = sys.modules.get("matplotlib.pyplot")
    if pyplot is not None:
        real_show = pyplot.show
        pyplot.show = lambda *args, **kwargs: None
    try:
        exec(compile(tree, "<exercise>", "exec"), __main__.__dict__, user_vars)
    finally:
        if pyplot is not None:
            pyplot.show = real_show
            pyplot.close("all")
    if expr is not None:
        user_vars["__check_result__"] = eval(expr, __main__.__dict__, user_vars)
        var = "__check_result__"
    for name in list(defines) + [var]:
        if name not in user_vars:
            raise NameError(name + " not defined")
    return user_vars[var]

def check_structure(code, rules=()):
    # Returns "" if the code follows every rule, otherwise a message saying what is missing
    import ast
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    nodes = list(ast.walk(tree))
    for rule in rules:
        if rule == "last_eq":
            last = tree.body[-1] if tree.body else None
            value = last.value if isinstance(last, ast.Expr) else None
            if not (isinstance(value, ast.Compare) and len(value.ops) == 1 and isinstance(value.ops[0], ast.Eq)):
                return "Your code should use == to compare the two sides of the Complement Rule."
            if ast.dump(value.left) == ast.dump(value.comparators[0]):
                return "The two sides of your == should be calculated in different ways."
        elif rule == "complement":
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.NotEq) or (isinstance(n, ast.UnaryOp) and isinstance(n.op, ast.Invert)) for n in nodes):
                return "Use a comparison operator like != to find the students who are not in the event."
        elif rule == "arithmetic":
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.BinOp) and isinstance(n.op, (ast.Sub, ast.Add)) for n in nodes):
                return "The Complement Rule relates an event to its complement through subtraction, e.g. 1 - P(not A)."
        elif rule == "no_replace":
            # Needs a random.choice(..., replace=False) call, so a hand-picked sample fails
            calls = [n for n in nodes if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Attribute) and n.func.attr == "choice"]
            if not calls:
                return "Use np.random.choice() to pick the residents at random."
            if not any(k.arg == "replace" and isinstance(k.value, ast.Constant) and k.value.value is False for c in calls for k in c.keywords):
                return "Make sure no resident can be picked more than once (set replace=False)."
        elif rule == "cluster_random":
            calls = [n for n in nodes if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Attribute) and n.func.attr in ("choice", "sample")]
            if not calls:
                return "Use np.random.choice() to pick the floors at random."
            # np.random.choice can pick the same floor twice unless replace=False
            for c in calls:
                if c.func.attr == "choice" and not any(k.arg == "replace" and isinstance(k.value, ast.Constant) and k.value.value is False for k in c.keywords):
                    return "Make sure the same floor cannot be picked twice (set replace=False)."
        elif rule == "df_sample":
            calls = [n for n in nodes if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Attribute) and n.func.attr == "sample"]
            if not calls:
                return "Use .sample() to pick the residents in each year at random."
            # replace=True can pick a resident twice (and sometimes happens not to, so check the code)
            if any(k.arg == "replace" and not (isinstance(k.value, ast.Constant) and k.value.value is False) for c in calls for k in c.keywords):
                return "Make sure no resident can be picked more than once (leave out replace, or set replace=False)."
            # A plain SRS of 20 gets exactly 10 of each year about 1 time in 8, so also
            # require the code to split the residents up by the "year" column
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.Constant) and n.value == "year" for n in nodes):
                return "Use the year column to split the residents into freshmen and sophomores first."
        else:
            raise ValueError("unknown structure rule: " + rule)
    return ""

def values_match(actual, expected):
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd
    if isinstance(expected, (pd.Series, pd.DataFrame)):
        actual, expected = [
            x.squeeze(axis=1) if isinstance(x, pd.DataFrame) and x.shape[1] == 1 else x
            for x in (actual, expected)
        ]
        if type(actual) is not type(expected):
            return False
        actual, expected = actual.sort_index(), expected.sort_index()
        if list(actual.index) != list(expected.index):
            return False
        if isinstance(expected, pd.DataFrame):
            last_level = lambda cols: [c[-1] if isinstance(c, tuple) else c for c in cols]
            if last_level(actual.columns) != last_level(expected.columns):
                return False
        try:
            return bool(np.allclose(actual.to_numpy(dtype=float), expected.to_numpy(dtype=float), equal_nan=True))
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            return False
    try:
        return bool(np.isclose(float(actual), float(expected)))
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return False
'

custom_checker <- function(label, user_code, solution_code, check_code, envir_result, evaluate_result, envir_prep, last_value, stage, ...) {
  # (learnr doesn't pass the last value of Python chunks, so we run the code)
  if (label %in% names(value_checks)) {
    if (stage != "check") return()
    spec <- value_checks[[label]]
    structure_msg <- tryCatch({
      helpers <- reticulate::py_run_string(checker_py, local = TRUE, convert = FALSE)
      reticulate::py_to_r(helpers$check_structure(user_code, as.list(spec$structure)))
    }, error = function(e) "")
    if (nzchar(structure_msg)) {
      return(list(message = paste(random_encouragement(), structure_msg), correct = FALSE))
    }
    correct <- tryCatch({
      helpers <- reticulate::py_run_string(checker_py, local = TRUE, convert = FALSE)
      get_result <- function(code) {
        helpers$get_result(code, var = spec$var, expr = spec$expr,
                           last_value = isTRUE(spec$last_value), defines = as.list(spec$defines))
      }
      values_match <- helpers$values_match
      # Student's code runs first, so if it modifies shared data the solution can't fill it in for them
      actual <- get_result(user_code)
      expected <- if (is.null(spec$value)) get_result(solution_code) else reticulate::r_to_py(spec$value)
      isTRUE(reticulate::py_to_r(values_match(actual, expected)))
    }, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (correct) {
      return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
    }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
  # Exact code checking (requires a <label>-solution chunk and <label>-code-check chunk)
  if (stage == "code_check") {
      if (user_code == solution_code){
          return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
      }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
}

gradethis_setup()
tutorial_options(exercise.completion = FALSE, exercise.checker = custom_checker, exercise.timelimit = 180,
                 exercise.reveal_solution = FALSE
)
```

```{python setup_py, include=FALSE}
# Hours studied per week by the 100 surveyed students (Populations vs. Samples)
study_hours = np.array([17, 35, 16, 20, 23, 24, 28, 22, 27, 12, 23, 21, 16, 20, 13, 16, 22, 17, 15, 12,
                        27, 28, 21, 21, 6, 28, 29, 26, 28, 10, 23, 12, 33, 14, 23, 23, 17, 17, 26, 28,
                        25, 28, 21, 16, 16, 21, 21, 37, 19, 32, 35, 21, 23, 16, 27, 22, 31, 20, 10, 27,
                        25, 21, 16, 25, 25, 28, 13, 35, 25, 23, 32, 30, 2, 24, 12, 24, 9, 22, 27, 25,
                        28, 26, 23, 9, 30, 27, 19, 17, 29, 18, 18, 22, 17, 35, 14, 31, 28, 26, 20, 13])

# Hours of sleep last night for all 60 residents of a dorm house (Simple Random Sampling)
sleep_hours = np.array([6.0, 7.3, 4.7, 8.7, 7.8, 6.6, 6.6, 7.4, 6.7, 6.7, 7.9, 7.6, 6.9, 6.9, 7.2,
                        6.3, 6.5, 7.7, 6.8, 5.4, 6.4, 7.8, 6.7, 6.8, 7.8, 9.2, 6.1, 8.6, 5.5, 7.2,

                        7.9, 9.6, 6.0, 10.0, 10.0, 8.9, 8.0, 6.2, 8.2, 6.5, 7.0, 6.7, 7.3, 8.5, 6.3])

# The same dorm as a data frame: only freshmen (first 36 rows) and sophomores (last 24) live there
# (Stratified Sampling)
dorm = pd.DataFrame({
    "year": ["Freshman"] * 36 + ["Sophomore"] * 24,
    "sleep_hours": sleep_hours
})

# The same dorm with a floor column: 6 floors of 10 residents, each with 6 freshmen and
# 4 sophomores (Cluster Sampling)
dorm_floors = dorm.assign(floor=list(range(1, 7)) * 6 + list(range(1, 7)) * 4)

# The same dorm with each resident's score on their most recent exam (Scatter Plots)
dorm_exams = dorm.assign(exam_score=[77, 81, 67, 76, 89, 76, 77, 77, 76, 74, 83, 83, 78, 83, 74, 82, 73, 81, 75, 71, 75, 86, 91, 74, 83, 78, 76, 87, 80, 88, 81, 88, 86, 83, 87, 82, 71, 77, 93, 88, 88, 83, 78, 78, 91, 80, 85, 69, 85, 91, 88, 78, 71, 82, 75, 76, 72, 77, 74, 77])
```

```{js mcq-cooldown, echo=FALSE}
// Cooldown on the "Try Again" button of multiple choice questions (radio buttons or
// checkboxes; numeric questions are not affected). The wait is 10 seconds after the first
// wrong answer to a question and 10 seconds longer after each one after that, up to 60.
// Attempts are saved in the browser so reloading the page doesn't reset the countdown.
(function() {
  var FIRST_WAIT = 10, EXTRA_WAIT = 10, MAX_WAIT = 60;  // seconds
  var KEY = "mcq-cooldown:" + window.location.pathname;
  var state = {};
  try { state = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY)) || {}; } catch (e) {}
  function save() { try { localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(state)); } catch (e) {} }
  var justSubmitted = {};

  // When a multiple choice answer is submitted, note it, so that a Try Again button
  // showing up afterwards counts as a new wrong attempt (and one that shows up after a
  // page reload doesn't)
  document.addEventListener("click", function(e) {
    var btn = e.target.closest && e.target.closest('button.btn-primary[id$="-action_button"]');
    var question = btn && btn.closest(".tutorial-question");
    if (question && question.querySelector('input[type="radio"], input[type="checkbox"]')) {
      justSubmitted[question.getAttribute("data-label")] = true;
    }
  }, true);

  function startCooldown(btn) {
    var question = btn.closest(".tutorial-question");
    if (!question || btn.dataset.cooldown) return;
    var id = question.getAttribute("data-label");
    if (justSubmitted[id]) {
      delete justSubmitted[id];
      var attempts = (state[id] ? state[id].attempts : 0) + 1;
      var wait = Math.min(FIRST_WAIT + EXTRA_WAIT * (attempts - 1), MAX_WAIT);
      state[id] = { attempts: attempts, until: Date.now() + wait * 1000 };
      save();
    }
    if (!state[id]) return;  // not a multiple choice question
    btn.dataset.cooldown = "true";
    var label = btn.textContent;
    (function tick() {
      var secondsLeft = Math.ceil((state[id].until - Date.now()) / 1000);
      if (secondsLeft > 0 && document.body.contains(btn)) {
        btn.disabled = true;
        btn.textContent = label + " (" + secondsLeft + "s)";
        setTimeout(tick, 250);
      } else {
        btn.disabled = false;
        btn.textContent = label;
      }
    })();
  }

  // learnr adds a new Try Again button (yellow, btn-warning) each time an answer is wrong
  var selector = 'button.btn-warning[id$="-action_button"]';
  new MutationObserver(function(mutations) {
    mutations.forEach(function(m) {
      m.addedNodes.forEach(function(node) {
        if (!node.querySelectorAll) return;
        if (node.matches(selector)) startCooldown(node);
        node.querySelectorAll(selector).forEach(startCooldown);
      });
    });
  }).observe(document.documentElement, { childList: true, subtree: true });
})();
```

<!-- ============================== Data Collection ============================== -->

## Sampling Populations

Throughout this course we have been working with datasets that are *samples* of a larger group---we very rarely have access to the entire population.
In this section we will discuss the differences between populations and samples, and how we might create those samples via different sampling methods.


### Populations vs. Samples

So what is the difference between a population and a sample? A **population** is the entire group of individuals or items that we are interested in studying, while a **sample** is a subset of that population that we actually collect data from.

The numerical characteristics of a population are called **parameters**, while those of a sample are called **statistics**. For example, the average height of all adults in the United States is a population parameter, while the average height of a sample of 100 adults is a sample statistic. See the table below for some common measures and their corresponding population parameters and sample statistics.

::: {.disttable .stattable}
| Measure | Population Parameter | Sample Statistic | Use |
|:----------|:----------:|:----------:|:------------------------------|
| Mean | $\mu$ | $\bar{x}$ | Measuring the center/location of a distribution |
| Standard Deviation | $\sigma$ | $s$ | Measuring the spread/scale of a distribution |
| Proportion | $\pi$ or $p$ | $p$ or $\hat{p}$ | Measuring the frequency of a binary variable |
:::

Suppose researchers at the University of Chicago want to know how many hours per week its undergraduates spend studying. To find out, a researcher goes to Regenstein Library at 10pm on a Tuesday and surveys 100 students about how many hours they study per week.

```{r q1, echo=FALSE}
question(

  answer("All students who were in Regenstein at 10pm on Tuesday", message = "The researchers want to learn about all UChicago undergraduates, not just the ones in Regenstein that night."),
  answer("The average number of hours UChicago undergraduates study per week", message = "This is a number describing the group, not the group itself."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

```{r q2, echo=FALSE}
  answer("All students who were in Regenstein at 10pm on Tuesday", message = "Only the 100 students who were surveyed gave us data."),
```

The hours studied per week by each of the 100 surveyed students are stored in a `numpy` array called `study_hours`. Use the cell below to look at the data more closely, and calculate the sample mean $\bar{x}$ and the sample standard deviation $s$ of `study_hours`. You can use the `numpy` functions `np.mean()` and `np.std()` to calculate these values. 

Note that by default, `np.std()` calculates the population standard deviation, so you will need to set the parameter `ddof=1` to calculate the sample standard deviation. Take a look at this [Khan Academy lesson](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/summarizing-quantitative-data/variance-standard-deviation-sample/a/population-and-sample-standard-deviation-review) to learn more about the difference between population and sample standard deviation.

### Sampling Methods

In order to use the sample to make plausible claim about the population, we need to make sure that the sample is representative of the population. There are several different sampling methods that can be used to achieve this, which we will review in this section.

#### Simple Random Sampling 

With this sampling method, every individual in the population has an equal chance of being selected for the sample. 
In practice, this can be achieved by using a random number generator or drawing names from a hat. 
We can implement Simple Random Sampling easily in Python using the `numpy` function `np.random.choice()`. Recall that we used `random.sample()` in lecture; these functions have similar functionalities, but one difference is that `np.random.choice()` samples with replacement by default, while `random.sample()` samples without replacement by default. 

For this example, let's imagine that our 100 student array `study_hours` is our *population* of interest, i.e., we only care about the 100 students who were studying in Regenstein at 10 pm on a particular Tuesday night. 
We can use the following code to take a simple random sample of 10 students from the `study_hours` array:

```{python srs-example, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
# Randomly pick 10 students; replace=False means no student can be picked twice
srs_sample = np.random.choice(study_hours, size=10, replace=False)

print(srs_sample)
print(np.mean(srs_sample))
```

Notice that if you run the code repeatedly, the sample and mean will change each time. This is because each student is equally likely to be selected, so the sample is random.

```{r q6, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "True or False: Choosing a random starting student and then taking every 10th student in `study_hours` after them is a simple random sample.",
  answer("True", message = "Every student does have the same 1 in 10 chance of being picked, but that isn't enough. Try again."),
  answer("False", correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! Every sample of 10 students is not equally likely: two students who are next to each other in the array can never be in the same sample. This method is called systematic sampling."),
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

Now let's try a different population. The array `sleep_hours` contains the number of hours of sleep that each of the 60 residents of a UChicago dorm got last night. Take a simple random sample of 15 residents from `sleep_hours` and save it as `sleep_sample`. Then calculate the sample mean and save it as `sleep_mean`.

```{python srs_ex, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}


```

```{python srs_ex-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
sleep_sample = np.random.choice(sleep_hours, size=15, replace=False)
sleep_mean = np.mean(sleep_sample)
```

#### Stratified Sampling 

With a stratified sample, the population is divided into subgroups (strata) based on certain characteristics, and a random sample is taken from each stratum. This ensures that the sample is representative of the population with respect to those characteristics.

Let's go back to the dorm from the previous question. Assume only freshmen and sophomores live in this dorm. Because students in different years might have different sleep habits, we want our sample to include the same number of students from each year. 

The data frame `dorm` contains the same 60 residents as `sleep_hours`, with a `year` column that says whether each resident is a `"Freshman"` or a `"Sophomore"`, and a `sleep_hours` column with the hours of sleep they got last night. Here are the first few rows:

```{python dorm-head, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
dorm.head()
```

Using the code template below, take a stratified sample of 10 freshmen and 10 sophomores from `dorm`, and save it as `strat_sample`.

```{python strat_ex, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
# Split the population into strata (separate data frames)
freshmen = ......
sophomores = ......

# Take a simple random sample from each stratum
fresh_sample = freshmen.sample(...)
soph_sample = sophomores.sample(...)

# Combine the samples
strat_sample = pd.concat([fresh_sample, soph_sample])

```

```{python strat_ex-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# Split the population into strata
freshmen = dorm[dorm["year"] == "Freshman"]
sophomores = dorm[dorm["year"] == "Sophomore"]

# Take a simple random sample from each stratum
fresh_sample = freshmen.sample(n=10)
soph_sample = sophomores.sample(n=10)

# Combine the samples
strat_sample = pd.concat([fresh_sample, soph_sample])
```

#### Cluster Sampling

The population is divided into clusters (often based on geography or other natural groupings), and a random sample of clusters is selected. All individuals within the selected clusters are then included in the sample.

Let's go back to our dorm. The dorm has 6 floors, numbered 1 through 6, and 10 residents live on each floor. Instead of tracking down individual residents all over the building, we could randomly choose 2 floors and survey *every* resident on those floors. Here, each floor is a cluster.

The data frame `dorm_floors` contains the same residents as `dorm`, plus a `floor` column that says which floor each resident lives on. Using the code template below, randomly choose 2 of the 6 floors, then save every resident who lives on one of those floors as `cluster_sample`. The `pandas` method `.isin()` will be helpful here: `df["col"].isin(value_list)` is `True` for each row whose value in `"col"` is in `value_list`.

```{python cluster_ex, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
# Randomly choose 2 of the 6 floors (the clusters)
chosen_floors = np.random.choice(......)

# Keep every resident who lives on one of the chosen floors
cluster_sample = dorm_floors[......]

```

```{python cluster_ex-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# Randomly choose 2 of the 6 floors (the clusters)
chosen_floors = np.random.choice([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], size=2, replace=False)

# Keep every resident who lives on one of the chosen floors
cluster_sample = dorm_floors[dorm_floors["floor"].isin(chosen_floors)]
```

```{r cluster_ex-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```


Note that **multistage sampling** is a combination of the above methods, where the population is divided into clusters, and then a random sample of individuals is taken from each selected cluster.

#### Convenience Sampling

The sample is selected based on ease of access or availability, rather than random selection. This method is often used in practice, but it can lead to biased samples that are not representative of the population.

```{r q9, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "Researchers want to learn some information about all UChicago undergraduates. Which of the following are convenience samples? Select all that apply.",
  answer("Surveying the first 50 students who walk into Regenstein on a Monday morning", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Surveying every student eating lunch in the dining hall closest to the researchers' office", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Asking the 30 students in the researchers' own DATA 118 section to fill out the survey", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Randomly drawing 50 student IDs from the registrar's list of all undergraduates", message = "Every undergraduate has an equal chance of being picked here, so this is a simple random sample."),
  answer("Randomly selecting 20 students from each class year", message = "This takes a random sample from each group, so it is a stratified sample."),
  answer("Randomly choosing 5 houses and surveying every resident in them", message = "This randomly picks whole groups and surveys everyone in them, so it is a cluster sample."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

### Bias

We must be careful about how we sample populations. Without care, several kinds of bias can arise, including **selection bias**, **non-response bias**, **response bias**, **survivorship bias**, and **undercoverage bias**. You can read more about each of these [here](https://ds1.datascience.uchicago.edu/09/4/biases.html). Once you've done that, answer the following question.

```{r q10, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "To learn how much UChicago undergraduates study, researchers email a survey to every undergraduate. Many students with the heaviest course loads are too busy to fill it out, so most of the responses come from students with lighter schedules. Which kind of bias does this survey suffer from?",
  answer("Non-response bias", correct = TRUE, message = "The students who didn't respond are different in a meaningful way (they study more) from the students who did."),
  answer("Response bias", message = "Response bias is about the answers people give being inaccurate, like underreporting embarrassing behavior. Here, the problem is who didn't answer at all."),
  answer("Survivorship bias"),
  answer("Undercoverage bias", message = "Undercoverage bias happens when some groups are left out of who gets surveyed. Here, every undergraduate was sent the survey."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```


## Experiments

In the previous section, we focused on how to collect a sample that represents the population, so that we could describe some characteristics of that population.
However, often we want to answer a different kind of question: not just *what* is happening, but *why*.

For example, suppose we find that dorm residents who sleep more also tend to get better grades. Does getting more sleep *cause* students to do better in their classes? Or is there some other variable, like courseload, that impacts both sleep and grades? 
To answer questions about cause and effect, we would need to run an **experiment**, where we apply a treatment (like getting 8 hours of sleep) to some individuals, and compare them to individuals who don't.

However, we should note that conducting an experiment is not always feasible or ethical.
Experiments are considered the gold standard for learning about cause and effect, but they require us to control what each person does.
How would we make sure that students in our sleep experiment actually sleep exactly 8 hours every night, or eat exactly what we tell them to for a whole quarter?
And for some questions, assigning a treatment would be harmful: we could never ethically tell a group of students to sleep only 4 hours a night to see whether their grades drop.

In cases like these, we often rely on **observational studies** instead, where we collect data on what people already do without changing anything about their behavior.
Observational studies can still tell us a lot, as long as we keep in mind that they show us *associations*, and we need to be careful before making conclusions about causation.


### Experimental Design

Experiments are designed to test hypotheses about cause and effect. In an experiment, we typically split participants into two groups: a **treatment group**, which receives the treatment or intervention, and a **control group**, which does not. We then compare the outcomes of the two groups to see if the treatment had an effect.

A well-designed experiment should have the following characteristics:

* Randomization: Participants are randomly assigned to treatment and control groups to reduce bias and ensure that the groups are comparable.
* Control: The control group serves as a baseline for comparison, allowing us to isolate the effect of the treatment. Often, the control group receives a placebo or standard treatment, rather than none at all.
* Replication: The experiment is repeated with multiple participants to ensure that the results are reliable and not due to chance.
* Blocking: Participants are grouped into blocks based on certain characteristics (like age or gender) before randomization, to ensure that these characteristics are balanced across treatment and control groups.

Suppose researchers want to know whether taking a 30-minute afternoon nap improves exam scores for the residents of our dorm. Each designed experiment below is missing one of the characteristics above. Choose which one in the following questions:

```{r q11, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "Residents get to choose whether they want to be in the nap group or not.",
  answer("Randomization", correct = TRUE, message = "Residents who choose to nap might already be different from those who don't. For example, they might have lighter course loads, which could also affect their exam scores."),
  answer("Control"),
  answer("Replication"),
  answer("Blocking"),
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

```{r q12, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "All 60 residents take a nap every afternoon, and the researchers check whether their exam scores went up.",
  answer("Randomization"),
  answer("Control", correct = TRUE, message = "Without a group that doesn't nap, we can't tell whether exam scores changed because of the naps or because of something else, like the second exam being easier."),
  answer("Replication"),
  answer("Blocking"),
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

```{r q13, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "The researchers randomly assign 2 residents to the nap group and 2 residents to a control group that spends 30 minutes each afternoon resting quietly in their rooms without sleeping.",
  answer("Randomization"),
  answer("Control"),
  answer("Replication", correct = TRUE, message = "With only 2 residents in each group, any difference in exam scores could easily be due to chance."),
  answer("Blocking"),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  post_message = "Congratulations! You have found the third secret word: DELETE."
)
```

Blocking might sound familiar: it uses the same idea as one of the sampling methods we saw earlier.

```{r q15, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "Suppose we block by class year (splitting residents into freshmen and sophomores, then randomly assigning half of each year to the nap group). Which sampling method is most similar to blocking?",
  answer("Stratified sampling", correct = TRUE, message = "In both, we split the individuals into groups first, then randomize within each group. Stratified sampling uses this to choose who is in the sample, while blocking uses it to choose who gets the treatment."),
  answer("Simple random sampling"),
  answer("Cluster sampling"),
  answer("Convenience sampling"),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

#### Blinding

In addition to the attributes above, experiments can also be **blinded**. In a blinded experiment, participants do not know whether they are in the treatment or control group. This helps to reduce bias in their responses and behavior. An experiment can be **single-blind**, where only the participants are unaware of their group assignment, or **double-blind**, where both the participants and the researchers interacting with them are unaware of the group assignments.

### Causality

Establishing causality, or showing that a change in one variable directly causes a change in another variable, is a key goal of experiments. Beyond our experiments, we also need:

* Theoretical justification: There should be a logical reason to believe that the treatment could cause the observed effect.
* Temporal sequencing: The cause must occur before the effect.
* Evidence of association: There must be a statistically significant relationship in the data between the treatment and the outcome.
* Elimination of alternate causes: There must be no other plausible explanations for the observed effect, which is why we need to control for **confounding variables**. More on these later.

```{r q16, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "At the end of the quarter, researchers survey the dorm residents once and find that students who report feeling more stressed also report sleeping fewer hours. One researcher argues that stress keeps students awake at night, while another argues that sleeping less makes students more stressed. Which requirement for causality is hardest to establish from this data?",
  answer("Temporal sequencing", correct = TRUE, message = "Because the survey only measured stress and sleep at one point in time, we can't tell which one changed first, so either could be the cause."),
  answer("Evidence of association"),
  answer("Theoretical justification"),
  answer("Elimination of alternate causes"),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```



## Introduction to Visualization in Python


### `matplotlib`

`matplotlib` is the most widely used library for making visualizations in Python. It can make almost any kind of static plot, including line plots, bar charts, histograms, scatter plots, box plots, and heat maps, and nearly every part of a plot (colors, labels, fonts, sizes) can be customized. Many other plotting tools, like `seaborn` and the `.plot()` method in `pandas`, are built on top of `matplotlib`, so learning it will help you understand those as well.

Most of the plotting functions we need live in the `pyplot` module, which is conventionally imported as `plt`:

```{python import-plt, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

If you want to see what `matplotlib` can do, check out the [`matplotlib` gallery](https://matplotlib.org/stable/gallery/index.html), which has examples of many different plots along with the code used to make them.

### What's in a Plot?

Every `matplotlib` plot is built from two main objects:

* **Figure** (usually saved as `fig`): the entire window or page that everything is drawn on. You can think of it as a blank canvas. The figure controls things like the overall size of the image, and it is what we save when we want to export a plot.
* **Axes** (usually saved as `ax`): an individual plot that lives on the figure, with its own x-axis, y-axis, and data. Most of the work of making a plot, like drawing the data, adding a title, and labeling the axes, is done by calling methods on `ax`.

The most common way to create both at once is with `plt.subplots()`. In the example below, we use the freshman and sophomore means that we calculated in the stratified sampling section to make a bar chart (more on each chart type in the next section). Notice that each line after the first one calls a method on `ax`:

```{python fig-ax-example, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}

# a 6 inch by 4 inch figure with one set of axes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4)) 

ax.bar(["Freshman", "Sophomore"], [7.06, 7.56]) # draw the data
ax.set_title("Mean Hours of Sleep by Year") # add a title
ax.set_xlabel("Year") # label the x-axis
ax.set_ylabel("Mean hours of sleep") # label the y-axis

plt.show()
```

A single figure can also hold more than one set of axes. For example, `fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)` creates a figure with two plots side by side, and `axes[0]` and `axes[1]` are the two `Axes` objects that we can draw on separately.

You may also see code that calls functions directly on `plt`, like `plt.bar()` and `plt.title()`, without ever creating `fig` and `ax`. In that case, `matplotlib` creates a figure and axes for you in the background and draws on them. This is quicker for simple plots, but working with `fig` and `ax` directly gives you more control, especially when a figure has multiple plots.

### Best Practices

Everyone has their own preferences when it comes to visualizations, but here are some best practices that will help you make clear, effective plots:

* **Choose the right type of plot for your data.** Different plots are suited to different kinds of data. For example, a bar chart compares categories, while a histogram shows the distribution of a numerical variable. We will look at several types of plots in the next section.
* **Label everything.** Every plot should have a title and labels on both axes, including units when there are any (e.g., "Hours of sleep" rather than "sleep_hours"). If a plot shows more than one group, add a legend.
* **Use color meaningfully.** Color should show something about the data, like which group a point belongs to, rather than just being decoration. Use the same color for the same group across all of your plots, and choose colors that are colorblind-friendly (`matplotlib`'s default colors and color maps like `"viridis"` are good choices).
* **Don't distort the data.** For example, the y-axis of a bar chart should start at 0, since the height of each bar is meant to represent its value. Starting it higher can make small differences look much bigger than they really are.
* **Keep it simple.** Avoid clutter like 3D effects, heavy gridlines, or extra decorations that make the data harder to read. Make sure text is large enough to read easily.
* **Write captions.** A short caption below a plot should explain what it shows and what the reader should take away from it, so that the plot makes sense on its own.
* **Save plots as PDFs.** PDFs are vector images, meaning they stay sharp no matter how far you zoom in, and they are easy to view and add to reports. You can save a figure with `fig.savefig()`:

```python
# bbox_inches="tight" trims extra white space
fig.savefig("sleep_by_year.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")  
```

## Types of Plots in `matplotlib`

In this section we will explore several common types of plots in `matplotlib`, including bar charts, histograms, box plots, scatter plots, and heat maps. For each type of plot, we will discuss when to use it, how to create it in Python, and how to interpret it.

### Bar Charts

A **bar chart** compares a numerical value across different categories, like the number of individuals in each group or the mean of a variable for each group. Each category gets its own bar, and the height of each bar shows its value. We already made one bar chart in the previous section; here is another that shows how many residents of our dorm are in each year:

```{python bar-example, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
# Count the residents in each year
year_counts = dorm["year"].value_counts()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.bar(year_counts.index, year_counts.values)
ax.set_title("Dorm Residents by Year")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of residents")

plt.show()
```

The first argument to `ax.bar()` is the categories, which go along the x-axis, and the second is the height of each bar.

```{r q17, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "Which of the following encoding channels do bar charts use to convey information?",
  answer("Length", correct = TRUE, message = "The length (height) of each bar shows its value, so we compare categories by comparing how long their bars are."),
  answer("Color", message = "Bars can be colored, but in a basic bar chart every bar is the same color."),
  answer("Angle"),
  answer("Shape", message = "Every bar has the same rectangular shape."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  post_message = "Congratulations! You have found the fourth secret word: UNLIKE."
)
```

### Histograms

A **histogram** shows the distribution of a single numerical variable. The range of the data is split into equal-width intervals called **bins**, and the height of each bar is the number of values that fall in that bin. Unlike a bar chart, the bars in a histogram touch, because the x-axis is a continuous number line rather than a set of separate categories.

Here is a histogram of the hours studied per week by the 100 students surveyed in Regenstein:

```{python hist-example, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.hist(study_hours, edgecolor="black")  # edgecolor outlines each bar so the bins are easy to see
ax.set_title("Hours Studied per Week")
ax.set_xlabel("Hours studied per week")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of students")

plt.show()
```

When reading a histogram, we usually look at the **shape** of the distribution (is it symmetric, or skewed with a long tail to one side?), its **center** (where most of the values are), its **spread** (how far the values range), and any unusual values. 

Run the code above to see the histogram. We didn't tell `ax.hist()` how many bins to use, so it chose a number for us.

```{r q18, echo=FALSE}
question_numeric(
  "How many bins does the histogram above have?",
  answer(10, correct = TRUE, message = "By default, ax.hist() splits the data into 10 bins."),
  min = 1,
  max = 100,
  step = 1,
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

We can choose the number of bins ourselves with the `bins` argument. The number of bins can change how a histogram looks quite a bit: too few bins can hide the shape of the data, while too many can make it look noisy. Change the code below to make the same histogram with 20 bins. 

```{python hist_bins_ex, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.hist(study_hours, edgecolor="black")
ax.set_title("Hours Studied per Week")
ax.set_xlabel("Hours studied per week")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of students")

plt.show()
```

```{python hist_bins_ex-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.hist(study_hours, bins=20, edgecolor="black")
ax.set_title("Hours Studied per Week")
ax.set_xlabel("Hours studied per week")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of students")

plt.show()
```


### Box Plots

A **box plot** (or box-and-whisker plot) summarizes the distribution of a numerical variable using five numbers, known as the **five-number summary**:

* **Minimum**: the smallest value.
* **First quartile ($Q_1$)**: the value that 25% of the data falls below.
* **Median**: the middle value, which 50% of the data falls below. It is also called the second quartile.
* **Third quartile ($Q_3$)**: the value that 75% of the data falls below.
* **Maximum**: the largest value.

The distance between the first and third quartiles, $Q_3 - Q_1$, is called the **interquartile range (IQR)**, and it measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

We can calculate the five-number summary for `study_hours` with `numpy`:

```{python five-number-example, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
print("Minimum:", np.min(study_hours))
print("Q1:", np.percentile(study_hours, 25))
print("Median:", np.median(study_hours))
print("Q3:", np.percentile(study_hours, 75))
print("Maximum:", np.max(study_hours))
```

In a box plot, the box stretches from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$, with a line inside it at the median. The lines extending from the box, called **whiskers**, reach out to the smallest and largest values that are within $1.5 \times IQR$ of the box. Any values beyond the whiskers are considered **outliers** and are drawn as individual points. (The `study_hours` data doesn't have any outliers, so here the whiskers reach all the way to the minimum and maximum.)

```{python box-example, exercise = TRUE, jupyter_compat = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.boxplot(study_hours)
ax.set_title("Hours Studied per Week")
ax.set_ylabel("Hours studied per week")
ax.set_xticks([1], labels=["Surveyed students"])

plt.show()
```

Box plots are especially useful for comparing the distributions of several groups side by side. To do this, we pass `ax.boxplot()` a list with one set of values for each group. Here we compare the hours of sleep for freshmen and sophomores in our dorm:

```{python box-groups-example, exercise = TRUE, jupyter_compat = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
freshmen_sleep = dorm[dorm["year"] == "Freshman"]["sleep_hours"]
sophomore_sleep = dorm[dorm["year"] == "Sophomore"]["sleep_hours"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.boxplot([freshmen_sleep, sophomore_sleep])
ax.set_title("Hours of Sleep by Year")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Hours of sleep")
ax.set_xticks([1, 2], labels=["Freshman", "Sophomore"])

plt.show()
```

```{r q19, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "Run the code above. The box for sophomores is taller than the box for freshmen. What can we conclude from this?",
  answer("The middle 50% of sophomores' sleep hours is more spread out than the middle 50% of freshmen's.", correct = TRUE),
  answer("More sophomores than freshmen live in the dorm."),
  answer("Every sophomore slept more than every freshman."),
  answer("The sophomores' sleep hours have more outliers."),
  answer("The interquartile range of sophomores' sleep hours is larger than the interquartile range of freshmen's.", correct = TRUE),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  post_message = "Congratulations! You have found the final secret word: HICCUP."
)
```

### Scatter Plots

A **scatter plot** shows the relationship between two numerical variables. Each individual is drawn as a point, with one variable on the x-axis and the other on the y-axis. Scatter plots help us see if there is an *association* between the two variables, and if so, its direction and strength.

Remember our question from the Experiments section about whether students who sleep more get better grades? The data frame `dorm_exams` contains the same residents as `dorm`, plus an `exam_score` column with each resident's score on their most recent exam. Let's plot sleep against exam scores:

```{python scatter-example, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.scatter(dorm_exams["sleep_hours"], dorm_exams["exam_score"])
ax.set_title("Hours of Sleep vs. Exam Score")
ax.set_xlabel("Hours of sleep")
ax.set_ylabel("Exam score")

plt.show()
```

The first argument to `ax.scatter()` gives the x-coordinates of the points, and the second gives the y-coordinates. When reading a scatter plot, we look at the **direction** of the relationship (do the points trend upward or downward?), its **form** (do they follow a straight line or a curve?), and its **strength** (how closely do the points follow that trend?). Here, residents who slept more tended to score higher on their exam. But remember that this is observational data, so it shows an association, not that more sleep *causes* higher scores!

We can also use color to show a third variable on a scatter plot. For example, we can draw the freshmen and sophomores in different colors to see whether the relationship between sleep and exam scores looks similar for both years. To do this, we call `ax.scatter()` once for each year, and give each call its own `color` and `label`. Then `ax.legend()` adds a key showing which color is which year.

Fill in the code below so that the sophomores are drawn in orange.

```{python scatter_color_ex, exercise = TRUE, jupyter_compat = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}

# split the population into freshmen and sophomore data frames
freshmen = ...
sophomores = ...

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.scatter(freshmen["sleep_hours"], freshmen["exam_score"], color="blue", label="Freshman")
ax.scatter(sophomores["sleep_hours"], sophomores["exam_score"], ..., label="Sophomore")
ax.set_title("Hours of Sleep vs. Exam Score")
ax.set_xlabel("Hours of sleep")
ax.set_ylabel("Exam score")
ax.legend()

plt.show()
```

```{python scatter_color_ex-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
freshmen = dorm_exams[dorm_exams["year"] == "Freshman"]
sophomores = dorm_exams[dorm_exams["year"] == "Sophomore"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.scatter(freshmen["sleep_hours"], freshmen["exam_score"], color="blue", label="Freshman")
ax.scatter(sophomores["sleep_hours"], sophomores["exam_score"], color="orange", label="Sophomore")
ax.set_title("Hours of Sleep vs. Exam Score")
ax.set_xlabel("Hours of sleep")
ax.set_ylabel("Exam score")
ax.legend()

plt.show()
```

### Heat Maps

Finally, a **heat map** shows a table of numbers using color, where each cell of the table is shaded based on its value. Heat maps make it easy to spot patterns across two categorical variables at once, like which combinations have the highest or lowest values.

For example, we can use the `dorm_floors` data frame from the cluster sampling section to find the mean hours of sleep for each combination of floor and year. The `pandas` method `.pivot_table()` builds this table for us, with one row per floor and one column per year:

```{python heatmap-example, exercise = TRUE, jupyter_compat = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
# Mean hours of sleep for each floor (rows) and year (columns)
sleep_table = dorm_floors.pivot_table(index="floor", columns="year", values="sleep_hours", aggfunc="mean")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 6))
heatmap = ax.imshow(sleep_table, cmap="viridis", aspect="auto")
fig.colorbar(heatmap, ax=ax, label="Mean hours of sleep")  # the key showing which color means which value

ax.set_xticks(range(len(sleep_table.columns)), labels=sleep_table.columns)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(sleep_table.index)), labels=sleep_table.index)
ax.set_title("Mean Hours of Sleep by Floor and Year")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Floor")

plt.show()
```

`ax.imshow()` draws each value in the table as a colored square, and `fig.colorbar()` adds a key showing which color corresponds to which value. Without a color bar, a reader has no way of knowing what the colors mean, so always include one! In the `"viridis"` color map, lighter (yellow) cells have higher values and darker (purple) cells have lower values.

`matplotlib` has many other built-in color maps, which you can browse in the [`matplotlib` color map documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/colors/colormaps.html). Make an addition to the code below to make the same heat map using the `"magma"` color map instead of `"viridis"`.

```{python heatmap_ex, exercise = TRUE, jupyter_compat = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
sleep_table = dorm_floors.pivot_table(index="floor", columns="year", values="sleep_hours", aggfunc="mean")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 6))
heatmap = ax.imshow(sleep_table, aspect="auto")
fig.colorbar(heatmap, ax=ax, label="Mean hours of sleep")

ax.set_xticks(range(len(sleep_table.columns)), labels=sleep_table.columns)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(sleep_table.index)), labels=sleep_table.index)
ax.set_title("Mean Hours of Sleep by Floor and Year")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Floor")

plt.show()
```

